extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of analytic geometry and conic sections (19th‑century mathematical readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Methods, theorems, and worked examples about polar reciprocals of conic sections, constructions (tangents, poles), and related analytic procedures (tangent equations, Maclaurin expansions) in analytic geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabola focus / principal vertex reciprocal secant theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If any system of conic sections have the principal vertex of a parabola for a common focus, the polar reciprocals of any two of them, taken with respect to the parabola, have a common secant which touches the parabola at that vertex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by eliminating variables from the pair of polar equations; presented as a theorem following algebraic elimination of x and y from the governing equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus of the pole of the chord determined by two radii vectors (given angle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any two radii vectores drawn from a fixed point in the plane of a conic section making a given angle, find the locus of the pole of the chord connecting their extremities using the indices of position m' and m'' of the radii and relations between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up the conic equation relative to axes through the fixed point, represent chord and radius by linear equations y = αx + β and y = m x, eliminate variables to obtain a quadratic whose roots are m' and m''. Use the relation m' - m'' = (tan of given angle)/(1 + m m') and substitute to obtain an explicit equation for the locus; the pole coordinates follow from the chord's polar equation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition / duality: polar reciprocals (director notion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each curve in a reciprocal pair can be considered either as the envelope of the poles of the points of the other or as the locus of the poles of the tangents of the other; two curves so related are called polar reciprocals with respect to the conic section which is called the director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use polar/pole duality: tangent at a point on one is the polar of the corresponding point of the reciprocal; numerous theorems follow from this envelope/locus relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure: reciprocal of a second‑degree curve with respect to a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a circle (radius as linear unit) and a conic A x^2 + 2B x y + C y^2 + 2D x + 2E y + F = 0, the polar reciprocal curve (coordinates a, b) is given by formula (5): (F C - E^2) a^2 + 2(DE - FB) a b + (FA - D^2) b^2 + 2(CD - BE) a + 2(AE - BD) b - (B^2 - AC) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: equate tangent at point (x',y') on original to polar of corresponding point (a,b); clear fractions and eliminate x',y' to obtain explicit second-degree equation for reciprocal. Interpret geometrically: reciprocals of segments intercepted by tangent on axes are coordinates of corresponding reciprocal point when director is circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of reciprocals when comparing equations (4) and (5) — list (1st–6th)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of immediate geometric consequences when comparing a conic and its reciprocal with respect to a circle: (1) If B' - AC = 0 then the reciprocal passes through origin (parabola ↔ passes through centre). (2) If D' - AF = 0 then one touches axis and the other is hyperbola with asymptote parallel, etc. (3) Special conditions on B,D,E produce axes parallelism. (4) When D = 0 and F = 0 axes correspond to tangent/normal and reciprocal is parabola with axis parallel to y. (5) If curve is concentric with director, reciprocals' axes coincide in direction and lengths of corresponding axes are reciprocal. (6) Polar of origin with respect to one reciprocal coincides with polar of centre of director with respect to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each numbered property is deduced by substituting special vanishing/coinciding coefficients into equations (4) and (5) and interpreting the resulting canonical forms (parabola, hyperbola, circle, asymptotes, axes relations). Examples and small algebraic checks are given in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special case: director centre coincides with focus ⇒ reciprocal circle
rubrics_metrics.description: If the centre of the director coincides with a focus of the given conic and conditions FB − DE = 0 and FA − D^ = FC − E^ (with possibly C' = ±A') hold, then the reciprocal curve is a circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a generalization: impose the stated coefficient relations in the general reciprocal formula (10)/(11) to obtain the circle equation; centers of the three curves (given, director, reciprocal) lie on same straight line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure: reciprocal of a second‑degree curve with respect to a general second‑degree director (general formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a director of general second degree (8) and a given curve (9), the reciprocal curve is obtained by equating the tangent at (x',y') on the given curve to the polar of corresponding point (X,Y) and eliminating x',y'; the explicit resulting equation is given (equation (10)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equation (10) is lengthy: it expresses the reciprocal as a quartic-like combination of director and given-curve coefficient polynomials and includes mixed products; follow the algebraic elimination process as in the circle case but with substituted director coefficients. Use centralization of axes to simplify to (11) when director is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director specializations: central director simplification and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When the director is a central conic and axes of director are chosen, many coefficients vanish (B' = E' = 0, F' = -1) and the general reciprocal (10) simplifies to (11), analogous to the circle case with analogous properties (focus-centre conditions can yield reciprocal circles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt conjugate diameters of director to simplify forms; several earlier properties (v, vii, viii) generalize with these simplifications and lead to geometric conclusions about asymptotes and conjugate diameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal with respect to a parabola (parabolic director) — formula and properties
rubrics_metrics.description: When the director is a parabola (normalizations A'=0,B'=0,C'=1,D'=1,E'=0,F'=0), the reciprocal equation reduces to formula (12): (B'^−AC)x^2 + 2(BD−AE)x y + (D'^−AF)y^2 + 2(CD−BE)x + 2(DE−FB)y + E'^−FC = 0, with distinct parabolic reciprocal properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This parabolic case is not strictly analogous to the circle case. The text lists parabolic-specific properties: e.g., when B'−AC = 0 reciprocal has asymptote parallel to director axis; when BD−AE = 0 axes parallel/perpendicular relations; other special coefficient vanishings give tangency/through-origin relations. Use coefficient substitutions to identify conic-type and geometric relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: finding equation of tangent to conic sections without limits/indeterminate forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive tangent equation by algebraic manipulation: put conic with vertex at origin in standard form (1) and a point (h,k) on it in form (2); subtract and eliminate to obtain a linear equation (4) which is tangential to (1). For parabola, ellipse, hyperbola explicit tangent equations (5)-(7) are given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method avoids infinitesimals and indeterminate expressions; specific tangent formulas are provided for parabola, ellipse, hyperbola, and for shifted-centre forms (6' and 7'). Use substitution x±a etc. to move origin to centre when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for choosing the double sign in perpendicular distance formula
rubrics_metrics.description: In the algebraic expression for the perpendicular distance p of a point (h,k) from a given line y = a x + b referred to axes rotated by angle θ, the ± sign is selected based on whether the point lies above or below the line: use + when k − (a h + b) is positive (point above), − when negative (point below), to make p positive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: compute coordinates of foot E on the line, compare ordinate differences PM and EM; the algebraic sign corresponds to geometric position so that p (a magnitude) remains positive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development of circular functions by Maclaurin's theorem (recursive derivative method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain Maclaurin expansions of tan x and sec x by successive differentiation using recurrence relations for the derivatives (U1, U2, ...), e.g., u = tan x gives recurrences for higher derivatives expressed as polynomials in lower derivatives; similarly for sec x. Evaluations at x=0 yield coefficients for the Maclaurin series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute successive derivatives symbolically, note parity patterns (even derivatives zero at 0 for tan), and derive coefficients (examples given: series for tan x and sec x up to several terms). The method avoids binomial/indeterminate coefficient techniques and is presented with explicit small-n numeric values as checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction: place conic given an angle, an interior point (to be centre), and major axis length
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an angle and a point within it, and given the major axis magnitude, place the conic so that the given point is the centre and the two given lines are tangents: draw a circle centered at the given point with radius equal to semi-major axis; its intersections with the tangents are feet of perpendiculars from foci on tangents; from these feet draw perpendiculars to get foci; conic determined by foci and major axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric construction: circle on semi-major axis as diameter gives circumferences where perpendicular feet lie; draw perpendiculars to tangents at those feet, find foci by intersection, then determine major axis as diameter through foci; points of contact chosen so lines to foci make equal angles with tangents. Remarks on number/type of solutions (two hyperbolas/ellipses etc.) depending on position relative to circle are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary about chords in a circle (construction fact)
rubrics_metrics.description: If any two chords are drawn in a circle, perpendiculars through their extremities will form a parallelogram whose diagonals pass through the centre of the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short elementary corollary with a simple elementary proof indicated; included as a geometric observation useful in constructions involving chords and perpendiculars.
